basis: All six compositions are Sm3TaO7 with zirconia added from 0 to 10 per cent, and the paper is on the thermophysical properties of ZrO2-Sm3TaO7 ceramics -- thermal barrier coating work rather than thermoelectrics. RE3MO7 is the weberite-type ordered anion-deficient fluorite, orthorhombic Cmcm for the larger rare earths, with alternating chains of TaO6 octahedra and eight-coordinate SmO8 polyhedra. The taxonomy had fluorite_oxide and pyrochlore but nothing for the 3:1 cation ordering, so re3mo7_weberite is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl and used here; the pyrochlore entry is the one to be careful of, since A2B2O7 and RE3MO7 have the same four-to-seven cation-to-anion ratio and differ only in how the cations order. [ref 2] gives Sm3TaO7 Cmcm (63) mp-1192238 at hull 0.003 with 1 ICSD reference, which matches both composition and expected setting but on a single reference. The block ranks SmTaO4 C2/c with 2 references first; that is the fergusonite-type orthotantalate, a different composition that no sample is at. Confidence is medium because one ICSD reference is thin and because the smaller rare earths in this family take a disordered defect fluorite instead, so the ordering should be checked against the diffraction pattern rather than assumed from the formula.

dopant_roles.site: the octahedral M site of the weberite-type framework
dopant_roles.basis: (Sm3TaO7)(1-y)(ZrO2)y for y from 0.02 to 0.10, five of the six compositions. Both parents are fluorite-derived, so zirconia dissolving into the Sm3TaO7 lattice is the expected behaviour and tetravalent zirconium sits most naturally on the pentavalent tantalum site with charge balanced by further anion vacancies. The alternative -- that the zirconia stays as a dispersed second phase and the material is a two-phase ceramic -- is also plausible for a thermal barrier coating, where a deliberate phase mixture is often the design, and the composition string writes it as a mixture rather than as a formula. Recorded at medium confidence for that reason; either way it lowers the thermal conductivity by adding disorder, which is the point.

basis: The compositions and the paper disagree, and I follow the paper. The six compositions are written Ti(1-x)WxO with x from 0.13 to 0.58, but the paper is titled Epitaxial Ti1-xWxN alloys grown on MgO(001) by ultrahigh vacuum reactive sputtering -- the anion is nitrogen, not oxygen, and the x values match the series exactly. So the material is the TiN-WN pseudobinary, a rocksalt nitride solid solution, and the host key O-Ti-W is a transcription artifact in which N became O. That also explains why [ref 2] can only offer Ti-W-O compounds -- Ti3(WO6)2, TiWO4, Ti7(WO5)6, all computed with no ICSD references -- none of which is a phase anyone grows epitaxially on MgO(001); no mp_id is recorded. The assignment is high confidence because the title is unambiguous, but two structural caveats belong with it. Rocksalt WN is not stable in bulk; it exists here because the alloy is grown epitaxially on a lattice-matched rocksalt substrate, so the tungsten-rich end of this series is a metastable film phase rather than an equilibrium one. And at x = 0.58 the alloy is past the composition where cubic TiWN films are usually reported to stay single-phase, so the upper compositions may contain a second phase.

dopant_roles.basis: The anion of every composition in this host is recorded as oxygen, but the paper measures Ti1-xWxN. Oxygen is not a constituent of the material; it is nitrogen misread. Recorded here rather than only in the basis so that a downstream reader who filters on host elements does not treat this as an oxide.

basis: Zinc oxide is 80 to 85 mole per cent of every composition and the paper is on the positive temperature coefficient of electrical resistivity in ZnO ceramics, so the material is a ZnO-based electroceramic with titania and nickel oxide additions and the transport is carried by the wurtzite ZnO matrix. This is the case the project README warns about with Al-O-Zn, and [ref 1] walks straight into it: TiZnO3 R-3 (148) mp-14142 is the ilmenite-type line compound of the Zn-Ti-O system, a real phase that describes the chemistry but not the material, which is Ti-and-Ni-modified zinc oxide. No mp_id is recorded from it. The caveat that keeps this at medium rather than high: titanium at 10 to 20 mole per cent is far past the solubility of titanium in ZnO, which is well under one per cent, so a Zn2TiO4 spinel second phase is certainly present, and in a PTC ceramic that grain-boundary phase is not incidental -- it is what produces the resistivity anomaly the paper reports. The host is not flagged mixed, because the wurtzite matrix is what a single structural label should name and splitting per composition would not separate the two phases, which coexist in every sample; spinel is listed as an alternative instead.

dopant_roles.site: the tetrahedral cation site of the wurtzite lattice, and the grain boundaries
dopant_roles.basis: NiO from 0.3 to 6 mole per cent across the six compositions. Nickel is divalent like zinc, so it adds no carriers; a little of it enters the wurtzite lattice substitutionally and the rest segregates to the grain boundaries with the titanium-rich phase, which is where a PTC ceramic does its work. The dual role is why the site field names both.

basis: All six samples are SrPt10P4 and the paper is titled Superconductivity in the ternary compound SrPt10P4 with complex new structure type -- so the compound is certain and the paper itself says the structure is new. Nothing in the taxonomy is close: at 1:10:4 this is far too metal-rich for the ThCr2Si2 or ZrCuSiAs families that hold most ternary alkaline-earth phosphides. srpt10p4_type is therefore proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl and used here, deliberately as a thin entry: it records the identity of the phase without asserting a space group, because neither reference block carries an entry at this composition and I will not invent one. [ref 2] returns three other Sr-Pt-P line compounds -- Sr(P3Pt2)2 C2/c mp-8507, Sr(PPt3)2 Pa-3 mp-1194990 and SrPPt P-6m2 mp-1217967, each with at most 1 ICSD reference -- and none of them is what was measured; no mp_id is recorded. Confidence is medium rather than high for the structure, though the compound identification itself is not in doubt: stage 2 cannot resolve this from a database and has to read the crystallography out of the paper.

Every composition is silicon with 4 to 6 atomic per cent phosphorus, some of it added as GaP, and one sample additionally alloyed with 5 per cent germanium; the papers are on the role of electron-phonon interaction in heavily doped fine-grained silicon, on heavily GaP- and P-doped Si0.95Ge0.05, and on high-performance n-type Ge-free silicon thermoelectrics. The material is degenerately n-doped silicon and the structure is diamond cubic, Fd-3m. I disagree with [ref 1], which returns SiP Cmc2_1 (36) mp-2798 as PRIMARY: that is the silicon monophosphide line compound, a layered orthorhombic semiconductor, and nothing here is at a 1:1 ratio. The reference is worth one qualification rather than simple dismissal, though -- 5 at.% phosphorus is above the equilibrium solubility limit in silicon, so SiP precipitates plausibly do form in these heavily doped samples, and the nanostructuring literature this work belongs to treats them as deliberate phonon scatterers. That makes SiP a probable minority second phase, not the host, and phosphorus is recorded as a host element here only because the 5 at.% cut lands right on the doping level.

dopant_roles.site: the tetrahedral site of the diamond lattice
dopant_roles.basis: Five of the six compositions carry GaP at 1.5 to 3.5 per cent. Gallium is the acceptor half of a co-doping pair: added as GaP it enters with an equal number of phosphorus donors, so it does not simply compensate them -- the pair raises the total impurity concentration and the alloy scattering without moving the net carrier count as fast, which is how these papers push the power factor of an already degenerate semiconductor. Stage 3 should treat the Ga and the matching P together rather than as independent levels.

dopant_roles.site: the tetrahedral site of the diamond lattice
dopant_roles.basis: Si0.95Ge0.05 in the single composition from the second paper. Germanium is isovalent with silicon and adds no carriers; five per cent of the site is the low-germanium end of the SiGe alloy line, present to scatter phonons by mass contrast. The third paper is explicitly Ge-free and is the comparison against it.

reference_disagreement: assigned sg [227], ICSD-backed references for this host report [205, 36, 55, 216]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: All six samples are WP2 and both papers are on the type-II Weyl semimetal -- thermal and electrical signatures of a hydrodynamic electron fluid, and departure from the Wiedemann-Franz law in WP2. The compound has two reported settings and the difference matters here more than usual: the noncentrosymmetric orthorhombic beta phase, Cmc2_1, is the Weyl semimetal, and the centrosymmetric C2/m form is not, because inversion symmetry is what decides whether the band crossings exist at all. The taxonomy carried osge2_monoclinic for the C2/m NbSb2-type structure but nothing for its noncentrosymmetric relative, so beta_wp2_type is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl and used here. I disagree with the ranking in [ref 2], which marks PW Pnma (62) mp-2420 with 5 ICSD references PRIMARY: that is the MnP-type monophosphide, a different compound, and no sample is at a 1:1 ratio. Within the diphosphide the block gives P2W Cmc2_1 mp-11328 at hull 0.000 with 3 ICSD references and P2W C2/m mp-11329 at hull 0.015 with 2, and the Cmc2_1 entry is the one taken. The C2/m form is recorded as a separate polymorph rather than as a thermal phase, since nothing suggests heating converts one into the other inside the 12-300 K window.

other_polymorphs.note: The C2/m alpha setting of WP2, 2 ICSD references against 3 for Cmc2_1. A genuine reported structure, but nothing here says it is reached by heating the beta phase, and it is not the semimetal the papers measure.

basis: The single composition is PrPb3 and the paper is on non-Fermi-liquid properties in the cubic Pr-based compound PrPb3 under magnetic field -- the paper calls the structure cubic in its own title. RPb3 rare-earth plumbides are the AuCu3 L1_2 type, Pm-3m, with the rare earth at the cube corners and lead on the face centres, and [ref 2] confirms it: PrPb3 Pm-3m (221) mp-20939 at hull 0.000 with 3 ICSD references. The other entries in the block are different Pr-Pb stoichiometries, not polymorphs. The cubic point symmetry is the whole reason this compound is studied: it leaves the praseodymium crystal field ground state non-magnetic and degenerate, which is what produces the quadrupolar physics and the non-Fermi-liquid behaviour. That ordering happens near 0.4 K, well below the 10 K measurement, so nothing is recorded in phases.

Two samples are written Tl4PbTe3 and four are Tl(10-x)Pb(x)Te6 with x near 2, which are the same thing at the same ratio -- Tl8Pb2Te6 is Tl4PbTe3 doubled. That is the Tl5Te3 family: the tetragonal I4/mcm framework in which a heavier cation replaces one fifth of the thallium, the same substitution that gives Tl9BiTe6, the taxonomy exemplar. [ref 2] confirms it with the exact composition -- Tl4Te3Pb I4/mcm (140) mp-20740 at hull 0.000 with 5 ICSD references, the only entry in the block. Both papers fit: the second is explicitly on Tl-X-Te compounds with X = Ge, Sn and Pb, which is that substitution series, and the first reports the high figure of merit these very heavy, very low thermal conductivity compounds are known for. The four compositions that vary x in the third decimal place are fine-tuning the Tl:Pb ratio to move the Fermi level, not changing the structure.

All six compositions are Y(1-x)UxPd3 with x from 0.2 to 0.4, and both papers are on the Kondo effect and the crossover in transport behaviour in that series -- this is the classic Y1-xUxPd3 non-Fermi-liquid system. YPd3 is the AuCu3 L1_2 type in Pm-3m, and uranium substitutes for yttrium on the corner site while the palladium framework is untouched, so the structure is unchanged across the whole range. [ref 2] returns only Y4UPd15 and YUPd6, both P4/mmm with no ICSD references: those are computed ordered supercells at x = 0.2 and x = 0.5, which is what a database does when asked to represent a random substitutional solid solution on a cubic lattice. They confirm the composition range is real but they are not the structure of these samples, and no mp_id is recorded. The chunk file flags this host as an isoelectronic series and that is recorded, though the label is only half right -- uranium and yttrium are both nominally trivalent here, but uranium brings 5f electrons and that is precisely the point of the experiment, so stage 3 should not treat the axis as electronically neutral the way it would treat Si for Ge.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: the corner A site of the AuCu3 L1_2 cell, the site YPd3 gives to yttrium
solid_solution_axis.note: U/(U+Y) as the chunk file reports it. The two share the site and the structure type is the same at both ends, so there is no parent compound to assign per composition in the usual sense. What changes across the axis is the 5f occupancy: at low x the uranium is a dilute Kondo impurity and at higher x the moments interact, and the crossover between those regimes is what both papers measure. So the axis is structurally inert and electronically the entire experiment.

basis: Every composition is PtTe2 or Pt1.01Te with a trace of silver, and PtTe2 is the 1T CdI2-type ditelluride: octahedrally coordinated platinum in layers held together by van der Waals contact, P-3m1. [ref 2] confirms it -- Te2Pt P-3m1 (164) mp-399 at hull 0.000 with 6 ICSD references, the strongest entry in the block. The Te4Pt3 and TePt entries are different compositions rather than polymorphs. PtTe2 is a type-II Dirac semimetal in this structure, and the second paper, on fine tuning of defects to enable high carrier mobility, is working on exactly the two defect knobs the compositions show: one per cent excess platinum and silver at the thousandth level.

dopant_roles.site: the octahedral metal site within the layer
dopant_roles.basis: Pt1.01TeAgx with x swept from 0.001 to 0.005 across five samples -- a very fine sweep, which is the fine tuning of the title. Silver has one fewer d electron than platinum and is a straightforward acceptor on the metal site. The alternative, that silver intercalates the van der Waals gap rather than substituting in the layer, is real for a layered ditelluride and would give the opposite doping sign, so the site is recorded at medium confidence and the paper should settle it. The first paper, on binary-phased nanoparticles, suggests silver may also be present as a separate metallic phase in those samples.

dopant_roles.site: the van der Waals gap between the PtTe2 layers
dopant_roles.basis: Pt1.01 in five of the six compositions, against stoichiometric PtTe2 in the sixth. Excess metal in a 1T ditelluride self-intercalates into the van der Waals gap rather than occupying an in-layer site, which donates electrons and pins the layers together. It is a host element in excess on a structurally defined void, so interstitial rather than non_stoichiometry.

basis: All six compositions are W(1-x)NbxSe(2-y)Sy with selenium dominant and sulfur from 0.2 to 0.5 of the chalcogen site, and the paper is on the thermoelectric properties of that series. This is the 2H tungsten dichalcogenide: trigonal-prismatic coordination, two layers per cell, P6_3/mmc, the same structure for WSe2 and WS2 and for every alloy between them, which is why the substitution changes the band gap without changing the prototype. [ref 2] returns only computed ordered W-Se-S arrangements -- W2Se3S, W2SeS3, W3(Se2S)2, WSeS and so on, all at hull 0.010 to 0.013 with no ICSD references and several flagged AMBIGUOUS -- which is what a database produces when asked to represent a random chalcogen solid solution in a supercell. They are not distinct phases and no mp_id is recorded from them. WSe2 is the tungsten dichalcogenide most prone to being reported in the 3R polytype, so stage 2 should confirm the stacking rather than assume 2H.

dopant_roles.site: the trigonal-prismatic metal site within the layer
dopant_roles.basis: W(1-x)Nbx with x from 0.02 to 0.06 across all six samples. Niobium has one electron fewer than tungsten, so it is an acceptor and makes these p-type; substituting on the metal site of a transition-metal dichalcogenide is the standard route to doping one, since the van der Waals gap offers intercalation as the only alternative and that is far less controlled.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: the chalcogen site of the 2H layer, which sulfur and selenium genuinely share
solid_solution_axis.note: S/(S+Se) across the six compositions. The chunk file does not flag this host as a solid-solution series, presumably because the spread is narrow, but it is one: these are WSe2-WS2 alloys at the selenium-rich end, and the second variable of the paper alongside the niobium level. The structure is the same at both ends, so the axis matters for the band gap and the alloy phonon scattering rather than for the prototype.

basis: Five of the six samples are Tb2S3 or TbS1.43, and the curator states the series as Tb2S3-x with x from 0 to 0.33 -- which is exactly the Th3P4 homogeneity range, running from Tb2S3 down to Tb3S4, TbS1.33. The second paper says so in its title: thermoelectric properties of Th3P4-type rare-earth sulfides Ln2S3. The gamma polymorph of the rare-earth sesquisulfides is the Th3P4 type in I-43d with ordered or disordered cation vacancies, and it is the one made for thermoelectrics because the vacancy concentration is the carrier-concentration knob, which is the subject of the first paper on the effect of non-stoichiometry. I disagree with [ref 2] here, which offers Tb2S3 Pnma (62) mp-9323 with 1 ICSD reference: Pnma is the alpha or beta sesquisulfide structure, and the papers explicitly make the gamma Th3P4 phase, so the reference is describing a polymorph of the chemistry rather than the material synthesised. The sixth sample is TbS, the rocksalt monosulfide from the third paper on TbS films, which is a different prototype at a different stoichiometry, so the host is flagged mixed and splits on the S:Tb ratio.

dopant_roles.site: the 12a cation site of the Th3P4 framework
dopant_roles.basis: Tb2S3-x with x from 0 to 0.33, which on the cation side is Tb(3-y)S4 with up to a third of a terbium per formula unit missing. Each vacancy removes three electrons, carrying the compound from metallic Tb3S4 to semiconducting Tb2S3 -- the same knob recorded for Nd-Te in this chunk and for La3-xTe4 in the taxonomy notes. It applies only to the Th3P4 compositions, not to the rocksalt monosulfide.

reference_disagreement: assigned sg [220], ICSD-backed references for this host report [225, 129, 62, 12]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: Four of the six samples are plain WS2 and the other two are WS2 with carbon added, and [ref 2] gives WS2 P6_3/mmc (194) mp-224 at hull 0.000 with 5 ICSD references as PRIMARY, which is the 2H polytype -- trigonal-prismatic tungsten, two layers per cell. The other two WS2 entries in the block are genuine polytypes rather than different compounds: R3m mp-9813 with 2 references is the 3R stacking, and P-3m1 mp-1028441 is the octahedral 1T layer. Neither is reached by heating 2H, so both are recorded as polymorphs rather than phases, but the 1T entry deserves attention rather than dismissal here: the first paper works on chemically exfoliated dichalcogenide nanosheets, and chemical exfoliation with lithium is the standard way of producing metallic 1T WS2. The chunk file also flags a film sample for exactly this reason. So the 2H assignment is right for the bulk majority, and the exfoliated samples may not be 2H at all -- that is a sample-level question this record cannot settle.

other_polymorphs.note: The 3R polytype, R3m, 2 ICSD references. Same trigonal-prismatic layer, three layers per cell instead of two; a stacking variant of the same prototype rather than a different structure type, and not produced by heating 2H.
The octahedral 1T layer. Produced by lithium intercalation and chemical exfoliation, which the first paper in this host does, and it reverts to 2H on annealing. Not a thermal phase.

dopant_roles.basis: WS2C0.02 and WS2C0.1, from the paper on enhanced thermoelectric properties of WS2 with single-walled carbon nanohorns. The carbon is a deliberate composite additive sitting between the WS2 grains, not a dopant in the lattice -- there is no site in a dichalcogenide for a carbon atom at ten per cent. It is recorded as a second phase so that stage 3 does not compute a doping level from it, and so that the host is not relabelled by the additive.

basis: Two compounds in equal numbers, and they are different structures. SrZn2Sb2, with three samples, is the CaAl2Si2 type: a trigonal P-3m1 Zintl phase in which strontium cations sit between corrugated Zn2Sb2 slabs of edge-sharing tetrahedra, and the first two papers are on the electronic structure and transport of AZn2Sb2 compounds and on polycrystalline SrZn2Sb2 specifically. [ref 2] carries it at Sr(ZnSb)2 P-3m1 (164) mp-7431, hull 0.000, 1 ICSD reference. SrZnSb2, also three samples and the subject of the third paper on the layered Zintl compound SrZnSb2, is the HfCuSi2 112 type -- anti-PbO ZnSb slabs alternating with flat square nets of antimony, given by the reference as Pnma (62) mp-12275 where the square net has distorted. The taxonomy had no entry for the 112 family, so hfcusi2_112_square_net is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl; it is listed as the alternative rather than the primary because the CaAl2Si2 id already existed and both papers on that half of the host predate the third. The host is flagged mixed and splits cleanly on the Zn:Sr ratio.

Three compositions and three prototypes. Si95Ti5, with three samples and the paper on synthesis and characterization of a bulk Si-Ti nanocomposite, is silicon with five atomic per cent titanium -- orders of magnitude above the solubility of titanium in silicon, so it is not an alloy but a diamond-cubic silicon matrix holding titanium silicide precipitates, which is what nanocomposite means in that title. It is taken as the primary on sample count and because the matrix is what carries the transport. Ti5Si3, two samples, is the Mn5Si3 D8_8 type in P6_3/mcm, given by [ref 2] as mp-2108 at hull 0.000 with 6 ICSD references. TiSi2, one sample, is the C54 type in Fddd, mp-2582 with 6 references -- and it is also the phase most likely to be precipitated inside the Si95Ti5 samples, so the host is genuinely mixed rather than merely heterogeneous. Confidence is medium because the paper list is a poor guide here: the first paper is on Mo5Si3 single crystals and the third on Cr1-xTixSi2 solid solutions, neither of which describes any composition in this host, so only the middle paper actually covers the material.

Six compositions spanning W0.05Ta0.95 to W0.85Ta0.15 and one paper, on the thermoelectric power of tantalum-tungsten alloys. Tantalum and tungsten are both body-centred cubic, adjacent in the periodic table and continuously miscible, so the whole series is one disordered A2 solid solution and the measurement is a rigid-band experiment: moving the electron-to-atom ratio from 5 to 6 sweeps the Fermi level through the bcc d band, which is what makes the thermopower worth measuring across the full range. [ref 2] returns Ta3W Fm-3m, TaW Cmmm and TaW3 Fm-3m, none with an ICSD reference -- computed orderings of a solution that is not ordered -- so no mp_id is recorded. No solid_solution_axis is recorded even though this is a complete substitutional series, because the two elements are in different groups and the substitution changes the electron count; the axis field is for isoelectronic series where the parent compound shifts, and here there is no compound, only an alloy.

Six uranium-zirconium alloys spanning U8.8Zr91.2 to U86Zr14, from a paper on the thermophysical properties of uranium-zirconium alloys -- metallic nuclear fuel rather than thermoelectrics. The solid solution label is right for the ends of the range and for the high-temperature phase: above about 950 K the system is a single body-centred cubic gamma solution across the whole join, and the zirconium-rich samples are hexagonal alpha-Zr solid solutions. But the 287-885 K window sits mostly below that, where the alloys are not single-phase. Two of the compositions, U27.6Zr72.4 and U23.87Zr76.13, lie in the field of delta-UZr2, which is an AlB2-type hexagonal phase and a genuinely different prototype, so alb2 is listed and the host is flagged mixed. The uranium-rich U86Zr14 would be orthorhombic alpha-U plus delta; the taxonomy has no alpha-U entry and none is invented for it. The second paper is a separate problem: its material is 45 per cent U in ZrH1.6, a uranium-zirconium hydride fuel, and the hydrogen never reached the composition string at all, so that sample is a uranium metal dispersion in a zirconium hydride rather than a U-Zr alloy -- interstitial_hydride is listed for it. Confidence is medium because the primary label is a simplification that the measured temperature range does not fully support.

Four of the five compositions are (Bi2O2Se)x(Ag)y from the paper on enhanced thermoelectric performance of Bi2O2Se with silver addition, so the host compound is Bi2O2Se -- fluorite-like Bi2O2 layers alternating with square selenium sheets -- and the silver is elemental metal added as a conducting second phase, not a constituent of the lattice. The fifth composition, BiAgOSe, is the silver member of the BiMOCh family from the second paper on substituting copper with silver in those layered compounds; that is the ZrCuSiAs 1111 structure, the BiCuSeO thermoelectric with silver on the copper site, and it is a different prototype, so the host is flagged mixed. I disagree with the solid-solution axis the chunk file reports, and the chunk file itself raises the CHECK that settles it: O/(O+Se) spanning 0.50 to 0.67 is not a substitution axis at all. In both of these structures oxygen belongs to the Bi2O2 layer and selenium to a separate sheet, and the two never share a site -- the ratio moves only because the silver content changes the normalisation. solid_solution_axis is therefore left null rather than recorded, and stage 3 must not treat oxygen and selenium here as competing for one sublattice.

dopant_roles.basis: Silver plays two different parts in this host and they must not be merged. In the four (Bi2O2Se)x(Ag)y composites it is metallic silver mixed in at 22 to 57 per cent of the written ratio -- a deliberate conducting second phase that raises the carrier concentration by contact rather than by entering the lattice, which is what addition means in that paper title. In BiAgOSe it is a lattice species on the tetrahedral site of the 1111 structure, occupying the position copper takes in BiCuSeO. Recorded as a second phase because that is what it is in four of the five compositions; the composition-level split will separate them.

basis: The five compositions are (Cu(1-x)AgxI)30(Ag2O)35(MoO3)35 and the paper evaluates the superionic properties of that ternary system. Written as oxide mole fractions, this is 30 per cent (Cu,Ag)I in 70 per cent of an Ag2O-MoO3 mixture at exactly the 1:1 ratio that is silver molybdate, Ag2MoO4 -- in other words the classic AgI-Ag2MoO4 fast-ion system, whose melt-quenched glasses are among the highest room-temperature ionic conductors known and which is the composition range most studied for exactly that reason. No crystal structure is assigned because a glass has none, and neither reference block returns anything for this host. Confidence is medium rather than high for one reason: the composition is stated but the preparation is not, and the same mixture slow-cooled gives a crystalline AgI plus silver molybdate composite instead of a glass, in which case the low-temperature end of the 294-444 K window would hold ordered beta-AgI and the high end the superionic alpha phase. The paper would settle it, and stage 2 should skip this host until it does.

All five compositions are (Ag0.2Cu0.8-d)2S0.7Se0.3 with the copper deficiency d swept from 0 to 0.02, and the paper is on p-type plastic inorganic thermoelectric materials -- the silver and copper chalcogenides that deform rather than fracture, whose plasticity comes from the weakly bound, mobile cation sublattice. The cation site is four fifths copper and the anion site is mostly sulfur, so this is a Cu2S-Cu2Se-Ag2S solid solution and the taxonomy entry for the antifluorite-like superionic copper chalcogenide is the right family. The 299-804 K window crosses the order-disorder transition of that family, which sits near 400 K in Cu2Se and somewhat lower in Cu2S, and above it the cations are liquid-like on a rigid anion lattice. What I cannot name is the ordered structure below the transition: the low-temperature phases of Cu2S and Cu2Se are large monoclinic superstructures, and for this particular quaternary mixture of both cations and both anions no specific ordered structure is established here, so the low-temperature phase is recorded as unresolved_crystalline rather than guessed at. The transition temperature is materials knowledge, not paper evidence, and is recorded at low confidence for that reason.

dopant_roles.site: the mobile cation sublattice
dopant_roles.basis: Cu0.8, 0.795, 0.79, 0.785 and 0.78 of the cation site across the five samples -- a deliberate copper deficiency of up to 2.5 per cent, and the only variable that distinguishes them. Removing copper from a Cu2X chalcogenide leaves holes behind, which is the standard and essentially the only way these compounds are p-doped. Stage 3 should read the deficiency as the doping level directly.

basis: All five compositions are Ag9GaS6 with selenium substituting up to a tenth of the sulfur, and the paper is on the thermoelectric properties of Ag9GaS6 with ultralow lattice thermal conductivity. Ag9GaS6 is an argyrodite: a rigid framework of GaS4 tetrahedra and chalcogen with nine silver ions distributed over far more crystallographic sites than they fill, which is exactly the origin of the ultralow thermal conductivity in the title. I disagree with [ref 1], which marks GaAgS2 I-42d (122) mp-5342 with 16 ICSD references PRIMARY: that is AgGaS2, the chalcopyrite nonlinear-optical crystal, and no composition here is at a 1:1:2 ratio. It is the best-known compound of the Ag-Ga-S system and therefore the one a formula-level lookup finds, but it is not what was measured; no mp_id is recorded from it. The argyrodites of this family order their silver sublattice on cooling and disorder it on heating, and the 299-806 K window almost certainly crosses that transition, so it is recorded -- but the temperature is materials knowledge rather than anything stated here and both phases carry the same prototype id, so the entry is at low confidence and exists mainly to tell stage 2 that two structures may be needed.

dopant_roles.site: the chalcogen sites of the argyrodite framework
dopant_roles.basis: Ag9Ga(S(1-x)Sex)6 with x from 0.03 to 0.10 in four of the five samples, the fifth being the pure sulfide. Selenium is isovalent with sulfur and adds no carriers; it is larger and heavier, so it expands the framework and lowers the lattice thermal conductivity further, and it also shifts the silver order-disorder transition, which is why the fully selenide member of this family transforms near room temperature while the sulfide does not.

reference_disagreement: assigned sg [33, 216], ICSD-backed references for this host report [122, 9]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: All five compositions are AgMnGeSbTe4 with up to four per cent Ag8GeTe6 added, and the paper is titled High Entropy Semiconductor AgMnGeSbTe4. The formula is the giveaway: four cations in equal amounts against four tellurium, which is a rocksalt lattice with tellurium on the anion site and silver, manganese, germanium and antimony sharing the cation site at random. It is the same architecture as the LAST and TAGS thermoelectrics, extended to four cations for the configurational entropy, and the entropy is doing structural work here -- GeTe on its own is rhombohedrally distorted at room temperature, and mixing four cations is what holds the structure cubic. high_entropy_alloy is listed as an alternative but is not the primary: that entry is for multi-principal-element metals on a simple lattice, whereas the ordered anion sublattice here makes this a semiconductor with a real gap, which is the point of the title. The Ag8GeTe6 additions at one to four per cent are argyrodite, a genuinely different structure, but they are a minor second phase rather than half the host, so the host is not flagged mixed. Neither reference block returns anything for this host and no mp_id is recorded.

The four compositions are AgPb2SbTe4, AgPb4SbTe6, AgPb6SbTe8 and AgPb8SbTe10, which is the AgPbmSbTe(m+2) series named in the second paper title -- the LAST-m thermoelectrics. Every member is cubic rocksalt: tellurium on the anion site, and silver, lead and antimony sharing the cation site, with the silver and antimony in equal amounts so the average cation valence stays at two. The series is famous for nanoscale silver- and antimony-rich regions inside that cubic matrix, which scatter phonons while leaving the lattice a single phase to diffraction, so the rocksalt label is correct at the structural level even though the material is not homogeneous at the nanometre scale. [ref 2] returns AgSb(Te8Pb7)2 I4/mmm mp-1229237 at hull 0.098 and AgSbTe3Pb Imm2 mp-1229036 at hull 0.468, neither with an ICSD reference: these are computed ordered supercells of a disordered rocksalt, one of them nearly half an eV per atom above the hull, and are not taken as the structure. No mp_id is recorded.

All five compositions are Ag2Se(1-x)Sx with x from 0.20 to 0.50, the last written Ag4SeS, and the first paper is on the superionic phase transition in silver chalcogenide nanocrystals while the second is on crystalline-structure-dependent mechanical and thermoelectric performance -- both are about the structure changing, not about a fixed one. Selenium is at least half the chalcogen site in every sample, so the ordered ambient phase is taken as orthorhombic beta-Ag2Se, naumannite. That is where the medium confidence comes from: Ag4SeS sits exactly at the crossover, and the ordered ambient structure of Ag2S is monoclinic acanthite rather than naumannite, so the sulfur-rich end may order differently; acanthite_ag2s, proposed in chunk 020, is listed as the alternative. The 294-472 K window crosses the superionic transition, which is near 407 K in pure Ag2Se and rises with sulfur content, so above it the material is the body-centred cubic phase with liquid-like silver. Because this is a solid-solution axis, that temperature moves with composition and the single value recorded cannot cover the whole host.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: the chalcogen sublattice of Ag2X, which sulfur and selenium genuinely share -- unlike the oxygen and selenium of the Ag-Bi-O-Se host in this same chunk, which do not
solid_solution_axis.note: S/(S+Se) as the chunk file reports it. The two end members have different ordered ambient structures -- orthorhombic naumannite for Ag2Se, monoclinic acanthite for Ag2S -- so this axis does change the prototype somewhere along it, which is unusual for an isoelectronic series and is why the assignment is medium rather than high. Both end members become the same body-centred cubic superionic phase on heating, and the transition temperature rises with sulfur content, so stage 3 must not apply one temperature across the series.

basis: The single composition is Ag8SiSe6 across all five samples, and the paper is on high electron mobility and disorder induced by silver ion migration. Ag8SiSe6 is the argyrodite in its textbook form -- the A8BX6 archetype itself, a framework of SiSe4 tetrahedra and selenium with eight silver ions spread over many more sites than they occupy -- and the silver ion migration named in the title is that disordered sublattice in motion. Neither reference block returns anything for this host, so the assignment rests on the formula and the paper and no mp_id is recorded. One temperature note rather than a phase record: these argyrodites order their silver sublattice below roughly room temperature and are cubic and disordered above it, and the measured window starts at 300 K, so the measurement sits essentially entirely in the disordered high-temperature phase rather than crossing into it. spans_transition is left false on that basis, but the margin is thin enough that stage 2 should resolve the cubic F-43m setting rather than an ordered low-temperature one.

All five compositions cluster tightly around Au49Al35Yb16 and both papers name the structure -- thermoelectric properties of Tsai-type Au-Al-RE quasicrystals with RE including Yb, and electronic density of states and metastability of icosahedral Au-Al-Yb. This is a Tsai-type icosahedral quasicrystal, built from the same rare-earth-bearing icosahedral cluster as the Cd-Yb archetype, and it is aperiodic, so there is no space group and no Materials Project entry to resolve. [ref 2] returns ordinary crystalline line compounds of the ternary -- YbAlAu Pnma mp-12784, YbAl7Au3, YbAl3Au -- none of which is the icosahedral phase; no mp_id is recorded and stage 2 must map this to an approximant and say so. Worth carrying forward from the second title: the icosahedral phase in this system is metastable and converts to its crystalline approximant on annealing, so the 17-883 K measurement may not have held one structure throughout.

Three compositions and three quite different materials. Al2Cu, two samples, is the theta phase and the prototype of the C16 structure type itself, tetragonal I4/mcm, which [ref 2] carries at mp-998 with 6 ICSD references; it is taken as the primary because it is the only composition here that is a definite single phase and because the third paper is on the thermal conductivity and resistivity of Al-Cu alloys. Cu76.12Al23.88, two samples, is at the other end of the binary: 24 atomic per cent aluminium in copper is past the limit of the face-centred solid solution, so the equilibrium state is alpha-Cu plus the gamma-brass Al4Cu9, and quenched it is a bcc-derived martensite -- this is Cu-Al shape memory alloy territory, and the first paper on cryogenic treatment of a copper alloy fits that. solid_solution_alloy is the closest available label for it; the taxonomy has no gamma-brass entry and none is invented here. Al57.7Cu37.7Fe3.5Si1.1 is the icosahedral Al-Cu-Fe quasicrystal of the second paper, on the low thermal conductivity of Al-based icosahedral quasicrystals. The host is flagged mixed and confidence is medium because none of the three is a majority and the Cu-rich pair cannot be resolved without knowing how they were cooled.

dopant_roles.site: an ordered site of the icosahedral Al-Cu-Fe cluster structure
dopant_roles.basis: Al57.7Cu37.7Fe3.5Si1.1, the single quasicrystalline sample. Iron is not a dopant here at all -- it is one of the three elements the icosahedral Al-Cu-Fe phase is made of, and the phase does not exist without it. It falls under the 5 at.% cut only because the cut is taken on the whole formula. Stage 3 should not compute a doping level from it.

dopant_roles.site: the aluminium sites of the icosahedral structure
dopant_roles.basis: 1.1 per cent in the same quasicrystalline sample. Silicon substitutes for aluminium in the icosahedral Al-Cu-Fe phase and is commonly added at about this level to widen the field over which the single quasicrystalline phase forms. It is a stabiliser rather than a dopant.

basis: All five samples are DyAl2, and both of the relevant papers are family surveys -- thermoelectric power of RAl2, and thermal conductivity of REAl2 compounds -- which is the strongest kind of evidence for a structure type, because a paper that measures a whole rare-earth series is relying on them all sharing one. The RAl2 compounds are the cubic C15 Laves phase, MgCu2 type, Fd-3m, and [ref 2] gives DyAl2 Fd-3m (227) mp-803 at hull 0.000 with 17 ICSD references -- the best-attested entry of any host in this chunk. The other Dy-Al entries are different stoichiometries rather than polymorphs. The ferromagnetic ordering near 60 K falls inside the 10-247 K window but is magnetic, not structural, and nothing is recorded for it.

The compositions are written (F(1-x)Rex)2VAl and the paper is on the effects of Re substitution on the thermoelectric properties of a pseudogap system. There is no fluorine here: F is Fe with the second letter lost, and the compound is Fe2VAl, the archetypal pseudogap full Heusler -- an L2_1 structure in Fm-3m whose valence electron count puts a deep pseudogap at the Fermi level, giving semiconductor-like thermopower in an intermetallic. That is one of the best-known thermoelectric Heuslers, so once the composition is read correctly the assignment is not in doubt, and the host key Al-F-V is a transcription artifact. Neither reference block returns anything, which is itself consistent with the host being chemically impossible as written; no mp_id is recorded.

dopant_roles.basis: Fluorine is not present in this material. The composition strings write iron as F, which is how a Heusler intermetallic came to be keyed as an aluminium fluoride. Recorded here so a downstream reader filtering on host elements does not treat this as a fluoride.

dopant_roles.site: the 8c iron site of the L2_1 cell, as the composition string writes it
dopant_roles.basis: (Fe(1-x)Rex)2VAl with x from 0.01 to 0.06 in four of the five samples. The site is taken from the composition string, which puts rhenium inside the iron parenthesis. It is recorded at medium confidence because the other natural reading for a pseudogap Fe2VAl study is substitution on the vanadium site, which is the usual way of shifting the electron count through the pseudogap, and the two readings put the dopant on different sublattices with different consequences for the band structure. The paper would settle it.

basis: All five compositions are Al70-71Pd20 with the balance made up of iron, manganese and rhenium, and two of the three papers say icosahedral in their titles -- improvement of thermoelectric properties of icosahedral AlPdRe quasicrystals, and thermal stability, electrical and magnetic properties of icosahedral Al-Pd-Mn. One composition carries an explicit _IQC suffix. Al-Pd-TM at seventy per cent aluminium and twenty per cent palladium is the icosahedral field of that system, and i-Al-Pd-Re in particular has the highest electrical resistivity of any metallic alloy, which is why it is measured thermoelectrically at all. The structure is aperiodic, neither reference block returns anything, and no mp_id is recorded; stage 2 must map this to an approximant and say so.

dopant_roles.site: the transition-metal sites of the icosahedral cluster structure
dopant_roles.basis: Al71Pd20Re3.15Fe5.85 in two samples. Rhenium is a defining constituent of the i-Al-Pd-Re phase, not an impurity in an Al-Pd-Fe one: it is what pushes the resistivity into the insulating range and it is named in the paper title. Iron partially replaces it here, so the pair should be treated as one transition-metal sublattice split between two species.

dopant_roles.site: the transition-metal sites of the icosahedral cluster structure
dopant_roles.basis: Al70Pd20Fe8Mn2 and Al70Pd20Fe6Mn4. Manganese is the transition metal of the best-known member of this family, i-Al-Pd-Mn, and these two compositions interpolate between the iron and manganese variants. Again a constituent rather than a dopant; stage 3 should not compute a doping level from it.

basis: Both compositions are Ce(x)La(1-x)Ru2Al10 with x of 0.1 and 0.3, and the first paper is on the anisotropic transport properties of CeRu2Al10 while the second is on the effects of Y and La doping on its magnetic ordering and Kondo behaviour. CeRu2Al10 is the exemplar of the taxonomy entry: the YbFe2Al10 structure type, orthorhombic Cmcm, in which the rare earth sits inside a large aluminium polyhedral cage. [ref 2] supports it without being able to name it -- La(Al5Ru)2 Cmcm (63) mp-1211269 at hull 0.000 is LaRu2Al10 in exactly the expected space group, though with no ICSD reference behind it. The cage and its rattling are why these compounds have low thermal conductivity, and the unusually high antiferromagnetic ordering temperature of CeRu2Al10, near 27 K, is inside the 10-314 K window but is magnetic rather than structural, so nothing is recorded in phases. Lanthanum dilution is precisely the experiment: replacing the cerium with a non-magnetic ion of the same size to separate the Kondo and cage contributions.

dopant_roles.site: the rare-earth site at the centre of the aluminium cage
dopant_roles.basis: Ce0.1La0.9 and Ce0.3La0.7 -- a tenth and three tenths of the rare-earth site, so alloying rather than dilute doping even though cerium falls under the 5 at.% whole-formula cut in a compound with thirteen atoms per formula unit. Cerium and lanthanum are both trivalent and nearly the same size, so the substitution is structurally inert; what cerium brings is the 4f electron, and the whole point of both papers is to watch the Kondo and magnetic behaviour appear as it is added. Recorded as substitutional rather than isoelectronic because the f occupancy is the variable, not a side effect.

reference_disagreement: assigned sg [63], ICSD-backed references for this host report [199]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: Three compositions and two quite different kinds of material. Al94.6Mg5.2Mn0.1Cr0.1 with two samples is a 5xxx-series aluminium alloy -- the paper is on an aluminium alloy for gravitational-wave antenna cryogenics -- and Mg91.39Al8.23Zn0.38 is an AZ-series magnesium alloy from the paper on Mg-Zn-rare-earth diffusivity; both are ordinary substitutional solid solutions, face-centred for the first and hexagonal for the second, and together they are three of the five samples, which is why solid_solution_alloy is the primary. Al3Mg2 with two samples is something else entirely: the beta Samson phase from the paper on the giant-unit-cell Al3.26Mg2 compound, a cubic Fd-3m structure with over a thousand atoms in its cell and intrinsic partial occupancy, which gives it a glass-like thermal conductivity in a binary of two light metals. The taxonomy had nothing for it, so beta_al3mg2_samson is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl and listed as the alternative, and the host is flagged mixed. [ref 2] ranks Mg17Al12 I-43m (217) mp-2151 with 5 ICSD references first; that is the gamma phase, a different composition from anything measured -- though it is genuinely relevant as the precipitate in the AZ-series magnesium sample, which is a second phase inside one composition rather than a host in its own right. Confidence is medium because the primary label covers three samples of two different lattices and leaves the most interesting composition to the alternative.

dopant_roles.basis: 0.1 atomic per cent in the 5xxx aluminium samples. Manganese has almost no solubility in aluminium at service temperature and is added to form Al6Mn dispersoids that control the grain structure; it is not in solid solution and not a dopant. Stage 3 should not compute a level from it.
0.1 atomic per cent alongside the manganese, and there for the same reason -- Al7Cr dispersoids for grain control in a 5xxx alloy. Same treatment.

dopant_roles.site: the hexagonal close-packed magnesium lattice
dopant_roles.basis: 0.38 atomic per cent in the single Mg91Al8Zn0.4 sample. Zinc is genuinely in solid solution in magnesium at this level and is the Z of an AZ-series designation; unlike the manganese and chromium above it is a dissolved solute rather than a dispersoid former, which is why the role differs.

basis: All five samples are Ni2MnAl and the paper names it outright -- exchange bias effects in Heusler alloy Ni2MnAl/Fe bilayers. X2YZ with a late transition metal at X is the full Heusler L2_1 structure, Fm-3m, and [ref 2] gives MnAlNi2 Fm-3m (225) mp-4922 at hull 0.000 with 3 ICSD references. One caveat is worth recording rather than leaving implicit: Ni2MnAl is the member of this family least willing to order. It quenches readily into the B2 structure, in which the manganese and aluminium share one site at random, and the B2 and L2_1 forms differ in their magnetism -- the disordered form is antiferromagnetic where the ordered one is ferromagnetic. The prototype is the ordered structure because that is what the compound is, but a sample measured here may well be partially B2, and only the paper can say. The other MP entries are different stoichiometries rather than polymorphs.

other_polymorphs.note: The quenched-in disordered form of the same compound, with Mn and Al sharing one site. Not a separate phase reached by heating so much as an incompletely ordered version of this one, which is why it is recorded here rather than in phases.

basis: Three quite different nitrides share this host and no single label covers them. Ti2AlN with two samples is the 211 MAX phase and Ti4AlN2.9 is the 413 member of the same nanolaminate series, together three of the five samples; [ref 2] gives Ti2AlN P6_3/mmc (194) mp-1080056 at hull 0.000 with 6 ICSD references, the best-supported entry for the host. Ti0.72Al0.28N is the cubic rocksalt solid solution (Ti,Al)N, the hard-coating material, with aluminium substituting on the titanium site of TiN. Al0.85Ti0.15N1.13 is the opposite end of that same tie-line and the second paper names its structure in its own title -- development and electrical properties of wurtzite (Al,Ti)N materials -- so it is titanium dissolved in AlN, not aluminium dissolved in TiN. The MAX phase is the primary because it carries the most samples and is the only one of the three that is a compound rather than a solid solution, but the host is genuinely mixed and must be split per composition. Film samples are present, which is consistent with the metastable rocksalt and wurtzite solid solutions: both are grown well beyond their equilibrium solubility by sputtering.

Both compositions are Ru2NbAl and the second paper says so in its title -- physical properties of the full Heusler-type Ru2-xFexNbAl. Ru2NbAl is one of the valence-electron-count 18 Heuslers whose pseudogap at the Fermi level gives semiconducting transport in an intermetallic, the same mechanism as Fe2VAl, and [ref 2] gives NbAlRu2 Fm-3m (225) mp-11537 at hull 0.000, which is the L2_1 structure in the right space group. The single ICSD reference behind it is thin, but the paper naming the structure type carries more weight than the reference count here.

dopant_roles.site: the X site of the L2_1 cell, which the composition string writes as Ru1.87Fe0.13
dopant_roles.basis: Ru1.87Fe0.13NbAl in one sample, and the paper title gives the series as Ru2-xFexNbAl, so iron is unambiguously on the ruthenium site. Iron has one electron fewer than ruthenium at the same site, so this moves the Fermi level down through the pseudogap and is a hole-doping knob rather than an incidental impurity; it also introduces the magnetic moment the first paper is about.

basis: Two Zintl phases in one host, and both are named in the paper titles. Sr5Al2Sb6 with three of the five samples is the 5-2-6 structure, chains of corner-sharing AlSb4 tetrahedra separated by strontium; Sr3AlSb3 with the other two is the 3-1-3 structure, isolated AlSb3 units. They are different prototypes at different electron counts and the host has to be split per composition. Two reference disagreements are worth stating rather than passing over. The taxonomy gives 5-2-6 as Pbam (55), the setting of Ca5Al2Sb6, while [ref 2] gives Sr5(AlSb3)2 Pnma (62) mp-28392 -- the 5-2-6 family really does come in more than one setting as the cation grows, so the strontium member may not be in the calcium one, and I would not assert Pbam here. The taxonomy gives 3-1-3 as Pnma (62) while [ref 1] gives Sr3AlSb3 Cmce (64) mp-17667; TEDesignLab is ICSD-backed and thermoelectric-specific, so on the project precedence its setting should be preferred over the taxonomy default for this compound. Both reference entries rest on a single ICSD reference each. Confidence is medium because the primary label covers three of five samples and the space group of neither member is settled.

dopant_roles.site: the tetrahedral framework cation site, in both the 5-2-6 and the 3-1-3 members
dopant_roles.basis: Sr3Al0.95Sb3Zn0.05 and Sr5Al1.95Zn0.05Sb6 -- one composition in each structure, each with the zinc written inside the aluminium stoichiometry. Zinc is divalent against trivalent aluminium, so replacing one for one removes an electron from a Zintl phase whose count is exactly balanced, and that is the entire experiment: these compounds are intrinsic semiconductors and this is the acceptor that makes them conduct. The role is substitutional rather than framework_substitution because the tetrahedral network here is an isolated polyanion rather than a cage enclosing a guest.

basis: Four of the five samples are ScAl2 or Yb-substituted ScAl2, and [ref 2] gives ScAl2 Fd-3m (227) mp-813 at hull 0.000 with 7 ICSD references -- the cubic C15 Laves phase, MgCu2 type. The fifth sample is ScAl3, which is not a Laves phase at all but the cubic AuCu3 L1_2 structure, and [ref 2] gives it separately as Pm-3m (221) mp-2121 with 5 ICSD references. The papers are on YbAl2 and on Yb1-xScxAl2, both of which are C15, so the scandium aluminide here is standing in as the isostructural non-magnetic partner of YbAl2 in a valence-fluctuation study. Confidence is medium because one composition sits in a different prototype and the host must be split.

dopant_roles.site: the A site of the C15 cell, the one at the centre of the Friauf polyhedron
dopant_roles.basis: Yb0.05, Yb0.1 and Yb0.15 of the rare-earth site in three samples. This reads as a dopant only because the 5 at.% cut is taken over the whole formula and there are three atoms in it; on its own sublattice ytterbium reaches fifteen per cent, which is alloying. It is also the active species rather than the impurity -- YbAl2 is the intermediate-valence end member and the point of the series is to dilute it with an isostructural trivalent partner, so stage 3 should not report this as a doping level.

basis: All five samples are SrAl4 single crystals and [ref 2] gives SrAl4 I4/mmm (139) mp-2775 at hull 0.000 with 4 ICSD references. That is the BaAl4 structure, and the taxonomy has no entry for it: thcr2si2_122 is its ordered ternary derivative, where the two crystallographically distinct sites of the BaAl4 framework are occupied by different elements. The space group, the body-centred tetragonal framework and the layer stacking are the same; what differs is that SrAl4 is the unsubstituted aristotype with aluminium on both sites. It is assigned here rather than being parked, with the gap recorded -- a baal4_type entry sitting above thcr2si2_122 would be the accurate arrangement and is worth considering at v4. The paper is on the Fermi surface and charge density wave of SrAl4, and that CDW near 240 K falls inside the measured 13-299 K window. It is not recorded in phases because a CDW is a periodic modulation of this structure rather than a transition to a different prototype, but it does mean a low-temperature refinement of these crystals would find a superstructure rather than the ideal I4/mmm cell.

Two oxidation states of americium in one host. AmO2 with three samples is the fluorite dioxide, Fm-3m, which every actinide dioxide takes -- the papers are on the thermophysical properties of NpO2, AmO2 and CmO2 and on modelling thermal conductivity in mixed oxide nuclear fuels, and the whole point of that literature is that these dioxides are one isostructural series. Am2O3 with two samples is the sesquioxide and is a different structure entirely. Which sesquioxide it is cannot be settled from the composition: the A-type trigonal form and the C-type cubic bixbyite form both occur for americium and which one is present depends on the thermal history, with A-type favoured at the high end of the 300-1468 K window measured here. Both are recorded as alternatives and a_type_re2o3 is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl to make that possible -- the taxonomy carried bixbyite and fluorite_oxide but had no A-type entry. Neither reference block returns anything for this chemistry, which is expected for a transuranic. Confidence is medium and the host must be split per composition.

All five samples are CeRu4As12 and the second paper names the structure in its title -- non-Fermi liquid behavior in the filled skutterudite compound CeRu4As12. The formula is the filled skutterudite archetype exactly: a Ru4As12 framework of corner-sharing octahedra with As4 rings, and cerium in the icosahedral void, in the LaFe4P12 structure. [ref 2] gives Ce(As3Ru)4 Im-3 (204) mp-1021508 at hull 0.000, which is that structure in its own space group, and Im-3 rather than the Im-3m of the empty framework is itself the signature of the filled variant. Cerium here is a constituent at full occupancy, not a partial filler, and it is the 4f electron it brings that makes this a Kondo semiconductor -- the first paper measures it as one.

Three of the five compositions are CoSb3-xAsx with the pnictogen total at three -- CoSb2.7As0.3, CoSb2.63As0.37 and the Ni-doped CoSb2.75As0.25 -- which is the binary skutterudite with arsenic alloyed onto the pnictogen rings, and the first paper is the classic survey of CoSb3 and related alloys. Yb0.30Co2.9Fe0.8Sb9As3.1 is the same framework with the void filled, so filled_skutterudite is an alternative for that composition. CoAsSb is not a skutterudite at all: the metal to pnictogen ratio is 1:2 rather than 1:3, which is the dipnictide field, and CoSb2 and CoAs2 both take the monoclinic arsenopyrite distortion of the marcasite type. That is why marcasite is listed as the second alternative, at lower confidence than the rest of this record -- the ordered ternary CoAsSb could equally sit in an ullmannite-like ordered pyrite derivative, as CoAsS does, and the third paper, an experimental and theoretical study of CoAsSb, would settle which. [ref 2] returns only Co2SbAs P-6m2 mp-1226441 at hull 0.055 with no ICSD reference, a computed entry at a different stoichiometry, and it does not support any of the three readings. The host is mixed across two and possibly three prototypes.

dopant_roles.site: the octahedral metal site of the skutterudite framework
dopant_roles.basis: Co0.99Ni0.01Sb2.75As0.25. Nickel has one electron more than cobalt on the same site and is the standard n-type dopant for CoSb3, used at exactly this dilution. A genuine dilute dopant, unlike the iron and ytterbium below.

dopant_roles.site: the octahedral metal site of the skutterudite framework
dopant_roles.basis: Yb0.30Co2.9Fe0.8Sb9As3.1 -- writing the framework as four metals, iron is a fifth of the metal site, not a dilute dopant. It falls under the 5 at.% cut only because the formula unit has sixteen atoms. In p-type filled skutterudites iron substitution is what creates the hole count that the filler then partly compensates, and the two are set together; the paper is on p-type skutterudites. Stage 3 should treat this as an alloying variable.

dopant_roles.site: the icosahedral void at the corner of the framework, partially occupied
dopant_roles.basis: Yb0.30 per four metal atoms in one composition. Ytterbium does not replace anything -- it occupies the empty void of the binary framework, donates its electrons to compensate the iron substitution, and rattles there, which is the mechanism that suppresses lattice thermal conductivity in this family. The role follows from the prototype and would be meaningless without it.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: the pnictogen site of the framework, the one that forms the planar four-membered rings
solid_solution_axis.note: Both are group 15 and both sit in the pnictogen rings, so the axis is real rather than an artefact of the element grouping. The spread reaches the midpoint, so the parent compound genuinely depends on the composition: at x of 0.08 to 0.12, where the median sits, this is CoSb3 with arsenic alloyed in, while CoAsSb at the top of the range is a different compound at a different metal to pnictogen ratio and is not on this axis at all. Stage 3 should assign the end member per composition and should exclude CoAsSb from the series.

basis: Every composition is LaFeAs1-xPxO1-yHy and the paper is on three superconducting phases with different categories of pairing in hydrogen-doped LaFeAsO. This is the 1111 iron pnictide, the ZrCuSiAs structure, P4/nmm -- alternating anti-PbO FeAs layers and fluorite-like LaO layers -- and it is the family in which iron-based superconductivity was first found. Neither reference block returns anything, which is unsurprising for a doubly substituted quaternary, but the structure type is not in doubt from the composition. Two distinct substitutions are running at once here and they do different things: phosphorus for arsenic inside the conducting layer, which is isovalent and acts by chemical pressure, and hydrogen for oxygen in the spacer layer, which is the electron-doping variable that replaced fluorine in this work and reaches much higher concentrations than fluorine can.

dopant_roles.site: the oxygen site of the LaO spacer layer, as a hydride anion
dopant_roles.basis: H0.25 and H0.30 per formula unit across all five compositions. Hydrogen is a host element of this key rather than a listed dopant candidate, but its role is the one thing that has to be recorded: it enters as a hydride ion on the oxygen site, and since it carries one negative charge where oxygen carries two, each substitution donates one electron to the FeAs layer. That is the doping variable of the whole paper, in the same way F-for-O is in LaFeAsO1-xFx, and it is not a processing residue despite being hydrogen in an oxide.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: the pnictogen site of the FeAs layer
solid_solution_axis.note: Arsenic and phosphorus share one site in the conducting layer and the substitution is isovalent, so it tunes the pnictogen height above the iron plane -- the structural parameter that controls the pairing in this family -- without changing the carrier count. The carrier count is set separately by the hydrogen. The axis spans the middle of the range rather than either dilute end, so no single parent compound applies to the host.

basis: All five compositions are ThFeAsN1-xOx and the paper is on the phase diagram of ThFeAsN. ThFeAsN is the nitride member of the 1111 family -- the ZrCuSiAs structure in P4/nmm, with anti-PbO FeAs layers alternating with ThN layers in place of the usual LnO ones -- and it is notable for superconducting near 30 K without any doping at all. The measured range of 10-35 K is a superconducting phase diagram rather than a transport window, which fits. The solid-solution axis printed for this host is a false positive and should be read as such: arsenic and nitrogen are both group 15, which is what triggered it, but they do not share a site. Arsenic is in the conducting FeAs layer and nitrogen is in the ThN spacer, so As/(As+N) is not a substitution axis at all and no sublattice fraction can be computed from it. The real substitution here is oxygen for nitrogen in the spacer layer, which is aliovalent electron doping rather than an isoelectronic series, so solid_solution_axis is left null and the substitution is recorded as a dopant role instead. This is the same trap the project already documents for O and Se in BiCuSeO.

dopant_roles.site: the nitrogen site of the ThN spacer layer
dopant_roles.basis: Oxygen runs from 0.2 to 0.6 of the spacer anion site across the five compositions -- an alloying range rather than a dilute one, and recorded as substitutional because it is aliovalent and is the variable of the paper. Oxygen carries two negative charges where nitrogen carries three, so each substitution removes an electron from the FeAs layer, and the isolated superconducting regions in the title are the result of moving along it. Not a processing residue and not a parse artefact, despite oxygen usually being one or the other in this dataset.

basis: Four of the five samples are Sr2VFeAsO3 and both papers are on superconductivity in perovskite-related iron-based materials. The compound is Sr2VO3FeAs, the 21113 phase: an anti-PbO FeAs layer, the same conducting slab as in every iron pnictide superconductor, separated from the next by a two-octahedra-thick Sr2VO3 perovskite block. [ref 2] gives Sr2VFeAsO3 P4/nmm (129) mp-1106248 with 3 ICSD references, confirming composition and space group together; the hull distance of 0.087 is normal for an intergrowth of two blocks that are each stable on their own and does not indicate a metastable phase. The taxonomy had no entry for this family -- zrcusias_1111 is the nearest, but its spacer is a single fluorite-like sheet rather than a perovskite block, and the difference is the reason these compounds are studied at all, since it makes the FeAs layers electronically isolated and adds a vanadium magnetic sublattice on top of the iron one. perovskite_blocked_fe_pnictide is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl. The fifth composition, SrVFeAsO3, is most likely the same compound with a strontium count lost in transcription; nothing sits at that stoichiometry.

The paper names the structure in its title -- synthesis and thermoelectric properties of Re3As6.6In0.4 with Ir3Ge7 crystal structure -- and the taxonomy already carries ir3ge7 for exactly that type. All five compositions are Re3As7 with small substitutions, and [ref 2] gives Re3As7 Im-3m (229) mp-2473 at hull 0.000 with 4 ICSD references, which is the Ir3Ge7 setting. The other MP entry, ReAs3 Fm-3m mp-1186907 at hull 0.650, is a computed structure far above the hull and is not what was made. The Ir3Ge7 type is a cage-like body-centred framework and the second paper treats these as new ternary arsenides for high-temperature thermoelectrics, which is consistent with the 76-963 K window.

dopant_roles.site: the arsenic framework site
dopant_roles.basis: Re3Sn0.1As6.9 and Re3Sn0.2As6.8 in four of the five compositions. Tin is written inside the arsenic stoichiometry and the total of the two stays at seven, so it takes framework sites rather than entering a void. Tin has fewer valence electrons than arsenic, so this is the hole-doping knob of the series and is the reason the compositions were made.

dopant_roles.site: the arsenic framework site
dopant_roles.basis: Re3As6.70In0.30, the composition named in the paper title. Indium plays the same role as tin and at a larger level -- three per cent of the formula -- again holding the seven-atom total, so the two should be treated as one substitution axis on the same site rather than as separate dopants.

dopant_roles.site: the rhenium site
dopant_roles.basis: Ni0.05Re3Sn0.2As6.8, a single composition at 0.5 per cent of the formula. Written outside the Re3As7 stoichiometry rather than inside it, so the site assignment is an inference from size and chemistry rather than from the string; nickel is far closer to rhenium than to arsenic in that respect. Dilute enough to be genuine doping, unlike the tin and indium above.

dopant_roles.site: the rhenium site
dopant_roles.basis: Co0.05Re3Sn0.2As6.8, the cobalt counterpart of the nickel composition and the same reasoning; the two were evidently made as a pair to compare two transition-metal substituents at one tin level.

basis: Both compositions are written as MgB2 with cobalt added -- (MgB2)1.5Co0.5 and (MgB2)1.7Co0.3 -- and the paper is on Co-addition into MgB2. MgB2 is the AlB2 structure, P6/mmm, graphene-like boron sheets with magnesium between them, and the taxonomy entry covers it directly. The cobalt is the reason confidence is medium rather than high: at these levels it is a quarter of the metal content, far beyond anything that dissolves in MgB2, and the word in the title is addition rather than substitution or doping. The realistic picture is MgB2 grains with cobalt and cobalt boride at the boundaries, so what was measured is a composite whose matrix is the AlB2 phase. That is recorded by naming composite_multiphase as an alternative rather than by flagging the host mixed, because there is one host phase here and a second constituent, not two competing structure assignments. [ref 2] returns only computed Mg-Co-B entries at hull distances of 0.14 and above with no ICSD support, none of them at a composition made here, and no mp_id is recorded.

dopant_roles.basis: Written outside the MgB2 unit in both compositions and present at ten to fifteen atomic per cent, which is why it is not in the dopant candidate list. Cobalt has almost no solubility in MgB2 -- what little enters the magnesium site depresses the superconducting transition sharply -- so the bulk of it must be a separate phase, most likely a cobalt boride formed during synthesis. Stage 3 should not compute a doping level from it.

basis: Three samples are EuB6 and two more are La-substituted EuB6, and [ref 2] gives EuB6 Pm-3m (221) mp-1077914 at hull 0.000 with 13 ICSD references -- the strongest reference support of any host in this chunk. That is the CaB6 type: a simple cubic array of europium with a B6 octahedron at the centre of every cell. The taxonomy entry names CeB6 as its exemplar, the same structure. EuB6 is measured here for its ferromagnetism and the colossal magnetoresistance near it; the ordering near 15 K sits inside the 10-297 K window but is magnetic, not structural, and nothing is recorded in phases for it. The other MP entry, EuB12 Fm-3m at hull 0.105, is a different stoichiometry in the UB12 family and was not made here.

dopant_roles.site: the cubic cation site at the corner of the cell, between the B6 octahedra
dopant_roles.basis: Eu0.9La0.1B6 and Eu0.8La0.2B6 -- a tenth and a fifth of the cation site, so alloying rather than dilute doping even though lanthanum falls under the whole-formula cut in a seven-atom cell. Europium is divalent in EuB6 and lanthanum is trivalent, so each substitution donates a carrier into a semimetal with a very low intrinsic carrier density; that is the experiment, and it also dilutes the magnetic sublattice at the same time.

basis: All five samples are UNi4B, measured as a single crystal in two of them, from papers on large thermoelectric power in metallic cerium and uranium compounds and on the magnetic phase diagram of hexagonal UNi4B. The compound is the CeCo4B type, an ordered derivative of CaCu5 in which boron replaces nickel in alternate basal layers, doubling the c axis and splitting the transition-metal site in two. The taxonomy had cacu5 and prni2al3_ordered_cacu5 but nothing for this ordering pattern, so ceco4b_ordered_cacu5 is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl. Confidence is medium and the reason is in the proposal: the ideal type is P6/mmm, but UNi4B itself has been refined in the polar P6_3mc and later in an orthorhombic Cmcm superstructure, and which is right matters here because the partial magnetic ordering this compound is famous for -- a third of the uranium moments staying paramagnetic to the lowest temperatures -- is a consequence of the site inequivalence that the ordering creates. [ref 2] offers nothing at this composition; its two entries, U2(Ni7B2)3 Fm-3m mp-10130 and UNiB4 I4/mmm mp-972320, are different stoichiometries with one ICSD reference each, so no mp_id is recorded.

Two thorium borides from one paper on the electrical properties of thorium borides: ThB4 with three samples and ThB6 with two. They are different structures and the host must be split. ThB6 is the CaB6 type, Pm-3m, and [ref 2] gives it as mp-1756 at hull 0.000 with 9 ICSD references -- good support, and cab6_hexaboride covers it. ThB4 is the UB4 type, tetragonal P4/mbm, built from B6 octahedra linked by B2 pairs, and it is assigned to ub12_boride because that entry names UB4 as its exemplar and AB12 / AB4 as its formula archetype. That is a weakness in the taxonomy worth flagging rather than using silently: UB12 is cubic Fm-3m and UB4 is tetragonal P4/mbm, so one entry is standing over two space groups and two distinct boron frameworks, and a separate ub4_tetraboride entry would be the accurate arrangement at v4. The primary is the tetraboride because it carries three of the five samples. [ref 2] also lists ThB12 Fm-3m mp-12570 with 2 ICSD references, which is the genuine UB12-type member of this chemistry but was not made here.

The compositions are Ba1-xKxBiO3 at x of 0.38 and 0.40, from papers on the thermoelectric power of superconducting Ba-K-Bi-O crystals and of Ba1-xKxBiO3. This is the cubic perovskite superconductor, Pm-3m, with bismuth on the octahedral site and barium and potassium sharing the A site. The composition matters for the structure: the undoped parent BaBiO3 is monoclinic because the bismuth octahedra breathe into alternating large and small sizes, a charge-ordering distortion that also makes it an insulator, and potassium substitution suppresses that distortion progressively until the structure becomes cubic near x of 0.37. Both compositions here sit just past that boundary, which is exactly where the superconductivity appears, so the cubic aristotype is the right assignment for what was measured rather than the distorted parent. [ref 2] returns nothing at this composition -- its entries are ordered line compounds such as KBa4Bi3O and KBa2Bi2O7 at quite different stoichiometries -- which is expected for a disordered solid solution on the A site, and no mp_id is recorded.

other_polymorphs.note: The breathing-distorted monoclinic form of the undoped parent BaBiO3. It is not reached by heating these compositions and is not a different prototype -- the same perovskite with a charge-ordering distortion -- but it is recorded so that a monoclinic reference entry for this chemistry is not mistaken for a contradiction.

dopant_roles.site: the octahedral B site
dopant_roles.basis: One composition, written (K1.00)(Ba1.00)3(Bi0.89Na0.11)4O12, from the third paper on the hydrothermal synthesis and crystal structure of a bismuthate. The string puts sodium inside the bismuth parenthesis, so the B site is where it goes, and a monovalent cation replacing bismuth is a strong acceptor. That is a different substitution from the potassium, which is on the A site, and the two should not be merged.

reference_disagreement: assigned sg [62, 167, 221], ICSD-backed references for this host report [140]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: All five samples are Ba1.9Ca2.4Mg9.7Si7 from a single paper that presents it as a new silicide Zintl phase. The composition is not a member of any structure type in the taxonomy: it is not the 5-2-6 or 3-1-3 or 9-4-9 Zintl stoichiometry, not CaAl2Si2, not Mg2Si, and the non-integer cation counts point to a large cell with mixed and partially occupied alkaline-earth sites rather than a line compound. Neither reference block returns anything. What can be said with confidence is the chemistry -- an electron-balanced silicide with two different alkaline earths and magnesium, which is the Zintl regime, and which is why it was measured for thermoelectric transport up to 983 K. What cannot be said from the composition alone is the structure type, and the paper is the only place it exists, since this is its first report. It is parked in unresolved_crystalline rather than forced into a Zintl entry it does not fit, and it is a clear candidate for the review queue: one paper would settle it and possibly yield a new prototype.

Every composition is YbBa2-xSrxCu3O7 and the paper is on structure and superconductivity in LnBa2-xSrxCu3O7. This is the 123 cuprate with ytterbium in place of yttrium -- the YBa2Cu3O7 structure, orthorhombic Pmmm, with CuO2 planes, a CuO chain layer and the rare earth between the planes -- and the whole LnBa2Cu3O7 series is isostructural, which is why substituting the rare earth is a standard experiment. The taxonomy entry is named for YBCO and covers it. [ref 2] does not return the 123 phase with ICSD support: its best-attested entries are BaYb2CuO5 Pnma mp-6323 and Ba4Yb(CuO3)3 Pm-3n mp-653337, which are the green-phase and related impurity compounds of this chemistry rather than the superconductor, and the one 123 entry it does give, Ba2YbCu3O7 Pmmm mp-1214570 at hull 0.040, carries no ICSD reference. The composition and the paper title decide this, not the reference ranking; that is the precedence the project sets and this host is a clean example of why.

dopant_roles.site: the barium site between the CuO2 plane and the CuO chain layer
dopant_roles.basis: Four compositions running from Sr0.1 to Sr0.3 of two barium atoms, which is five to fifteen per cent of that site -- alloying rather than dilute doping, and the variable named in the paper title. Strontium is isovalent with barium and smaller, so this is chemical pressure: it contracts the lattice without changing the carrier count, which is a way of separating the structural and doping contributions to the transition temperature. The oxygen content stays at seven throughout, confirming that the carrier count is not what is being varied.

reference_disagreement: assigned sg [47], ICSD-backed references for this host report [62, 65, 223]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: All five samples are Ba8Cu12.8Zn11.2P28.8 from a paper whose title is itself the warning -- breaking the tetra-coordinated framework rule: new clathrate Ba8M24P28. The compound is unambiguously a clathrate: eight barium guests in cages built from a covalent framework of copper, zinc and phosphorus, which is the structural definition and the reason it was made. What does not fit is the arithmetic of type I. An ideal type-I framework has 46 atoms enclosing 8 guests, and this one has 52.8 -- the extra framework atoms are exactly the rule the title says is broken, since a tetrahedral framework cannot accommodate them and some of the phosphorus must be three-coordinate instead. So clathrate_i is assigned as the nearest and most likely relative, at medium confidence, with the discrepancy recorded rather than smoothed over: stage 2 should not force these compositions into a 46-atom type-I cell, and the paper is needed to establish the actual framework. Neither reference block returns anything for this chemistry.

dopant_roles.site: the transition-metal sites of the covalent framework
