The two disilicides are not the same structure: CrSi2 is the hexagonal C40 type, P6222, while TiSi2 is the orthorhombic C54 type, Fddd, and the two are only partially miscible, so a series that runs from 20 to 80 per cent titanium on the metal site passes from one to the other. C40 is recorded as primary because CrSi2 is the thermoelectric member of the pair and the series is written as substitution into it, with tisi2_c54 as the alternative and the host marked mixed; the split is by the Cr:Ti ratio, with the crossover somewhere near the middle and a two-phase field around it, which is why confidence is medium rather than high. Titanium and chromium are adjacent but not isovalent, so this is not an isoelectronic axis and the chunk file flags none. I disagree with [ref 2]: its five entries are computed Ti-Cr-Si ternaries at stoichiometries such as Ti2Cr4Si5 and Ti3Cr17Si12, none with an ICSD reference and none matching a disilicide solid solution, so no mp_id is recorded.

The curator details settle this: a W-10Cr-1Hf alloy in weight per cent, ball-milled for 28 h and spark plasma sintered, plus a low-alloyed W-3Cr-2HfC, and the paper is on the microstructure and phase stability of a W-Cr alloy prepared by spark plasma sintering. Tungsten and chromium are both body-centred cubic and form a continuous solid solution at high temperature, so mechanical alloying followed by fast sintering gives a supersaturated bcc W(Cr) single phase -- which is exactly why phase stability is in the title, since the system has a miscibility gap at lower temperature and wants to decompose. solid_solution_alloy is the right entry rather than an ordered compound, and I disagree with [ref 2] on that point: CrW Cmmm (65) mp-1226162 at hull 0.124 with no ICSD reference is a computed ordered structure at a 1:1 ratio, neither the composition nor the state of these samples, so no mp_id is recorded. This is a fusion plasma-facing material measured for thermal transport rather than a thermoelectric candidate.

dopant_roles.basis: Hafnium is at 0.76 and 1.83 atomic per cent, and the curator names the second material W-3Cr-2HfC, so the hafnium is added as hafnium carbide. In this class of alloy HfC is a deliberate dispersoid: fine particles that pin grain boundaries and getter oxygen during milling, sitting as a discrete second phase rather than dissolving in the bcc lattice. Not a dopant, and stage 3 should compute no substitutional level for it.

basis: All five compositions are alpha-CsCu5Se3 or its antimony-substituted variants, and the paper is the discovery paper: alpha-CsCu5Se3 as a low-cost bulk selenide with high thermoelectric performance. No entry in v3 covers a ternary alkali copper chalcogenide at this stoichiometry, so acu5q3_layered is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl and used here. The compound identity is not in doubt; the structure is the uncertain part, and the reference block shows why. [ref 2] returns three neighbouring compositions -- Cs3(Cu4Se3)2 C2/m (12) mp-1188128, Cs2Cu5Se4 Cmcm (63) mp-28467 and CsCuSe4 P2_12_12_1 (19) mp-17095 -- and not one of them is CsCu5Se3, so the Cmcm setting recorded in the proposal comes from materials knowledge of the alpha form rather than from either reference, and no mp_id is taken. Confidence is medium on that basis. The alpha prefix in the paper implies a second modification of the same compound, so the 326-989 K window may cross a transition; nothing in the chunk file flags one and none is entered in phases, but it is the first thing to check against the paper.

dopant_roles.basis: Four compositions are Cs(Cu1-xSbx)5Se3 with x from 0.01 to 0.04, written with antimony inside the copper bracket, so it substitutes on the copper site of the anionic framework. Sb3+ for Cu1+ adds electrons and is the carrier-concentration knob of the paper, which needs one because the undoped compound is a very low-carrier p-type semiconductor.

basis: All four compositions are Ni1-xCuxFe2O4 with x from 0.4 to 0.6, and both papers are thermoelectric power studies of copper-substituted nickel ferrites. AB2O4 with two trivalent irons per divalent cation is the cubic spinel, Fd-3m, and the Ni-Cu ferrites are an inverse spinel series in which the divalent cations take octahedral sites and iron is split between both sublattices; the hopping conduction that the Seebeck data reflects is Fe2+ to Fe3+ on the octahedral sublattice. As with the Cd-Fe-Ni-O host, I disagree with [ref 2], which offers Fe4CuNiO8 C2/m (12) mp-1225235 at hull 0.083 with no ICSD reference -- a computed cation-ordered monoclinic cell where the real material is a cation-disordered cubic spinel, so no mp_id is recorded and the space group is taken as 227. One caution for stage 2: copper-rich ferrites tetragonally distort to I4_1/amd through the Jahn-Teller Cu2+ ion, and at x = 0.6 that is near the onset, though it is a distortion of the spinel prototype rather than a different one.

The single composition is CuFeSe2 and the first paper calls it chalcopyrite outright, in a study of cobalt-doped Cu1-xCoxFeSe2, while the second makes CuFeSe2 nanocrystals. CuFeSe2 is the mineral eskebornite and it belongs to the chalcopyrite family -- a diamond-like framework of corner-sharing tetrahedra with copper and iron ordered on the cation sublattice. The two references agree with each other and both disagree slightly with the ideal type, which is worth recording: [ref 1], ICSD-backed, gives FeCuSe2 in space group 112, and [ref 2] gives P-42m (111) mp-1079566 with 2 ICSD references, where ideal chalcopyrite is I-42d (122). That is not an error in the references -- eskebornite really is reported in a lower-symmetry chalcopyrite-derived tetragonal ordering rather than in the CuFeS2 setting -- so the assignment is the chalcopyrite family with the caveat that the space group is a derivative, and confidence is medium for that reason. The hull distance of 0.128 in the 2019 dump also looks unphysical for a mineral that exists, which is the usual dump artefact for these chalcogenides.

Four of the five samples are Cu6Fe4Sn12Se32 and two of the papers name the structure for us -- one on the structural and thermoelectric properties of Cu6Fe4Sn12Se32 single crystals, the other explicitly on selenospinel Cu6Fe4Sn12Se32. A selenospinel is the spinel prototype with selenium on the anion sublattice, so that is the assignment; note the cation count, 22 metals to 32 selenium against 24 to 32 for an ideal AB2X4, which makes it a cation-deficient spinel and explains the variable-range-hopping conduction and very low thermal conductivity the third paper reports. The fifth sample is Cu2FeSnSe4, a different structure: the tetragonal stannite type, which [ref 1] gives ICSD-backed as FeCu2SnSe4 I-42m (121) mp-22612 at hull 0.040 with 3 references. So the host is mixed and splits on the Se:metal ratio. Confidence is medium on the primary because the reference block backs only the stannite member, while for the selenospinel [ref 2] offers computed cells at hull 0.036 to 0.041, one of them flagged AMBIGUOUS and containing cadmium that is not in any composition here; no mp_id is recorded for the spinel.

Every composition is (La,Pr)2-xSrxCuO4 and the papers are on the solid-state chemistry of high-temperature oxide superconductors and on the structural and superconducting properties of La1-xPrSrxCuO4. That is the T-phase cuprate, K2NiF4 or Ruddlesden-Popper n = 1 in I4/mmm: single CuO2 planes separated by rock-salt (La,Pr,Sr)O layers, the parent of La2-xSrxCuO4 itself. The 12-79 K window is a thermopower measurement through the superconducting transition. Two structural notes that stay inside the prototype rather than splitting it: this family has an orthorhombic Bmab distortion below a few hundred kelvin from octahedral tilting, and praseodymium substitution of the kind used here is what pushes such cuprates towards the low-temperature tetragonal tilt pattern instead -- both are tilt variants of one n = 1 RP structure. No reference entry is offered for this quaternary and no mp_id is recorded.

dopant_roles.basis: Strontium appears in all five compositions at 0.1 to 0.3 per formula unit on the rare-earth site of the rock-salt block. In a cuprate this is not an ordinary dopant but the doping variable itself: Sr2+ for La3+ puts holes into the CuO2 plane and sets where the sample sits on the superconducting dome, which is what both papers are measuring. Stage 3 should treat the computed level as the hole count per copper.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: rare-earth site of the rock-salt block
solid_solution_axis.note: La/(La+Pr) over 5 compositions. Isovalent substitution on the A site, used to shrink the block and change the octahedral tilt rather than to dope, so the parent compound depends on the composition. Note this axis is independent of the strontium hole doping recorded in dopant_roles -- both act on the same site.

basis: Every composition is PbTe with a copper chalcogenide added, written as (PbTe)x(Cu2Te)y or PbTe(Cu2Se)0.09, and the curator transcribes three of them as percentages of PbTe plus Cu2Te. The first paper is on PbTe-based composites, so the samples are a rocksalt PbTe matrix -- which carries the transport and is what a Seebeck coefficient here measures -- with a few per cent of a second phase in it. rocksalt is therefore the primary with composite_multiphase as the alternative and the host marked mixed, rather than calling the whole thing a composite and losing the matrix. Confidence is medium because how much of the copper is dissolved in the PbTe and how much is a discrete Cu2Te or Cu2Se phase is a real question rather than a formality: copper is highly mobile in PbTe and partly enters interstitially, which is the synergistic role the third paper is about, while the second paper reports deliberate Sb and CuTe core-shell nanostructures. No reference entry is offered for this ternary and no mp_id is recorded.

dopant_roles.basis: Selenium appears only in PbTe(Cu2Se)0.09, where it arrives as part of the Cu2Se addition rather than being added on its own. Recorded as a second-phase constituent for that reason, with the caveat that some of it will dissolve into the matrix and sit isoelectronically on the tellurium site as PbTe1-xSex; which fraction does so cannot be decided from the formula, so confidence is low and stage 3 should not read a clean anion-substitution level from it.

Antimony appears only in (PbTe)81Sb2Te3Sb0.6(Cu2Te)5, which carries both an Sb2Te3 addition and excess elemental antimony, and the paper for it reports coherent Sb/CuTe core-shell nanostructures. So the antimony is there as a deliberate nanoprecipitate for strain and phonon scattering, not as a substitutional donor on the lead site.

basis: All three compositions are Cu12Sb4-xTexS13 with x near 1.8, and the first paper is on the crystal structure, electronic band structure and high-temperature thermoelectric properties of exactly that substitution. Cu12Sb4S13 is tetrahedrite, cubic I-43m, a large cell built from copper in both tetrahedral and trigonal-planar coordination with antimony in trigonal pyramids and a sulfur at the centre of the copper cluster. Tellurium substitutes antimony on that pyramidal site; Te4+ for Sb3+ donates an electron, which fills the hole in the copper-sulfur band and turns a metallic tetrahedrite semiconducting -- that is the whole point of going to x near 2, and it is why the substitution sits so close to a fixed value rather than sweeping. Tellurium is at 6 atomic per cent, just above the 5 per cent split, so it is not a listed dopant candidate and dopant_roles is empty; its role is substitutional on the antimony site. No reference entry is offered for this quaternary and no mp_id is recorded.

Four of the five compositions are Cu2SnSe3-xSx, and the third paper is on boosting the thermoelectric performance of Cu2SnSe3. Cu2SnSe3 is the Cu2GeSe3 structure type: a monoclinic diamond-like framework of corner-sharing tetrahedra, ordered on the cation sublattice, and that entry is the assignment for those four. The fifth, Cu4Sn7.5S14Se2, is a different compound -- the paper for it is on solid solution Cu4Sn7.5S16 -- in which tin is octahedrally coordinated rather than tetrahedral. Nothing in v3 covers that, so cu4sn7s16_type is proposed in prototypes_proposed.jsonl and recorded as the alternative rather than parking a real named compound in unresolved_crystalline; its rhombohedral setting is provisional, since the chunk file gives no reference entry for the formula. The host is mixed and splits on the Sn:Cu ratio, 1:2 against nearly 2:1. Confidence is medium for the host label because of that split, not because of doubt about Cu2SnSe3.

dopant_roles.basis: Two compositions carry indium at 3 to 7.5 per cent of the tin site, written inside the formula as Cu2Sn1-xInxSe3-yS y. In3+ for Sn4+ removes an electron, so it is the p-type acceptor for Cu2SnSe3 and is the band-engineering route the third paper takes. A straightforward substitutional dopant on the tetrahedral cation site.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: anion site of the tetrahedral framework
solid_solution_axis.note: S/(S+Se) over 5 compositions. Sulfur and selenium are both group 16 and share the anion sublattice, so this is a genuine isoelectronic axis -- but the top of the range, x = 0.87, is the Cu4Sn7.5S14Se2 composition, which is a different structure rather than the sulfur-rich end of one series. The axis is therefore only meaningful across the four Cu2SnSe3-xSx members, where it runs to about x = 0.3.

basis: The compositions are DyVO3 and Dy1-xCaxVO3 with x up to 0.2, and the paper is on transport and magnetic properties in Dy1-xCaxVO3 ceramics. DyVO3 is a GdFeO3-type orthorhombic perovskite and [ref 2] carries it at DyVO3 Pnma (62) mp-25144, hull 0.000, though on 1 ICSD reference. This host is a clean example of the reference describing the chemistry rather than the sample: the best-attested entry in the block by a wide margin is DyVO4 I4_1/amd (141) mp-18784 with 9 ICSD references, which is a zircon-type orthovanadate with V5+ in isolated tetrahedra -- a different stoichiometry, a different oxidation state and not a perovskite at all. Every composition here is written ABO3 with V3+ or mixed V3+/V4+, so the perovskite is the assignment and the space group taken is 62, not 141. The 10-338 K window crosses the magnetic and orbital ordering of the vanadate, which in the DyVO3 end member carries a monoclinic distortion; that is a symmetry lowering within the prototype rather than a new one.

dopant_roles.basis: Four compositions are Dy1-xCaxVO3 with x from 0.05 to 0.2, calcium on the A site. Ca2+ for Dy3+ is an acceptor that converts V3+ to V4+ and drives the series towards the metallic side of a Mott transition, which is what the transport measurement is following.

basis: All five compositions are Er1-xHoxNiSb and the paper title says half-Heusler phases Er1-xHoxNiSb outright. RNiSb with a heavy rare earth is the MgAgAs structure, cubic F-43m: the 18-electron half-Heusler with one of the four interpenetrating sublattices left empty, which is what makes it a semiconductor rather than a metal. Erbium and holmium are neighbouring trivalent lanthanides of nearly the same radius, so substituting one for the other keeps the structure and the electron count untouched and acts only on the phonons -- mass and strain fluctuation scattering on the rare-earth site -- which is why the whole series was measured to 994 K. No reference entry is offered for this quaternary and no mp_id is recorded.

solid_solution_axis.shared_site: rare-earth site of the half-Heusler cell
solid_solution_axis.note: Er/(Er+Ho) over 5 compositions spanning most of the range. Both are trivalent lanthanides on the same site, so the substitution is isovalent and the parent compound depends on the composition; the purpose is mass-fluctuation phonon scattering rather than doping.

basis: All four compositions are Sr2ErRuO6 with or without lanthanum on the strontium site, and the second paper names it: the high-temperature thermoelectric properties of the double-perovskite ruthenates. A2BB-prime-O6 with erbium and ruthenium alternating on the octahedral sites is the B-site ordered double perovskite, and the ordering here is strongly driven -- Er3+ and Ru5+ differ in both charge and size, which is exactly the condition that gives rock-salt ordering rather than a disordered B site. [ref 2] agrees and is ICSD-backed: Sr2ErRuO6 P2_1/c (14) mp-6294 at hull 0.000 with 3 references. The monoclinic rather than cubic setting is expected, since strontium with these B cations leaves a tolerance factor below one and the octahedra tilt on top of the ordering.

dopant_roles.basis: Three compositions are (Sr1-xLax)2ErRuO6 with x from 0.05 to 0.2, lanthanum on the A site. La3+ for Sr2+ is a donor, reducing Ru5+ towards Ru4+, and in a wide-gap double perovskite measured to 1250 K that is the way to raise a very low carrier concentration -- the first paper describes the same thing for the yttrium analogue.

reference_disagreement: assigned sg [87, 225], ICSD-backed references for this host report [14]. Confidence downgraded by verify_assignments.py; a disagreement can still be correct where the reference describes the chemistry rather than the sample.

basis: The single composition is Er2SbO2, better written Er2O2Sb, and the second paper is a review of the crystal chemistry of the rare-earth pnictide oxides (RE,Ca)mPnnOm with Pn = Sb or Bi. These are layered: fluorite-like Er2O2 slabs alternating with square nets of antimony, which is the Bi2O2Se arrangement -- the same anti-ThCr2Si2 stacking with the rare-earth oxide layer in place of Bi2O2 and a pnictogen net in place of the selenium one. The hypervalent square net is what makes the compound interesting, and the first paper is on decoupling electrical conductivity from the Seebeck coefficient in this family. Two reasons for medium confidence. [ref 2] gives Er2SbO2 Imm2 (44) mp-1225518 at hull 0.000 but with no ICSD reference, an orthorhombic distortion rather than the tetragonal I4/mmm parent -- plausible rather than wrong, since for a small rare earth the antimony net can dimerise, which is a distortion within this prototype. And the rest of the block is different chemistry entirely: Er2Sb2O7, Er3Sb5O12, Er3SbO7 and ErSbO4 are oxide-rich phases with Sb5+, not pnictide oxides with a reduced antimony net. No mp_id is recorded.

The compositions are EuMnO3, Eu0.8Sr0.2MnO3 and Dy0.2Eu0.8MnO3, with a fourth written Dy0.0Eu1.0MnO3 which is EuMnO3 again with a zero coefficient left in. The third paper is on the structural, transport and magnetic properties of RMnO3 perovskites and [ref 2] confirms the structure ICSD-backed at EuMnO3 Pnma (62) mp-25667, hull 0.000, 3 references. Worth the discrimination: the RMnO3 series splits by rare-earth size, and for holmium and smaller the hexagonal YMnO3 structure takes over, which the taxonomy carries separately. Europium is on the large side of that boundary, so the orthorhombic tilted perovskite is right here and ymno3_hexagonal would be wrong. Two other entries in the block to set aside: EuMn2O5 Pbam and Eu2Mn2O7 Fd-3m are different stoichiometries, and the EuMnO3 Pm-3m entry at hull 0.046 is the untilted aristotype, not what a Eu3+ A site gives. The robust window is 12-298 K; the 1364 K upper span is an outlier from the thermal study rather than a transport curve.

dopant_roles.basis: Eu0.8Sr0.2MnO3 puts strontium on the A site, and the first paper is on the Eu1-xSrxMnO3 series. Sr2+ for Eu3+ is an acceptor: it creates Mn4+ alongside Mn3+ and sets up the double-exchange and charge-ordering physics the magnetic and electrical measurements are after.

Dy0.2Eu0.8MnO3 comes from the paper on Dy1-xEuxMnO3, so dysprosium and europium are the two ends of one isovalent rare-earth series rather than a host and a dopant. Both are trivalent, so no carriers are added; what changes is the A-site radius and hence the octahedral tilt, which is what modifies the low-temperature magnetic interactions the paper reports. Recorded as isoelectronic substitution rather than as substitutional doping for that reason, and the level stage 3 computes is an alloy fraction.
